title: Your first freight brokerage hire should solve the real bottleneck
seoTitle: Your first freight brokerage hire should solve the real bottleneck
searchIntent: Who should a freight brokerage hire first?
excerpt: Choose the first role by studying the work that occupies the owner, then define a handoff the new person can own.
takeaway: Choose the responsibility before the job title. The right first hire creates useful capacity without adding work the operation cannot support.

sections.title: Do not assume the first hire should sell.
paragraphs: Luis challenges the idea that another salesperson is automatically the next step for a busy brokerage. More demand can make an existing operating constraint worse. If current shipments already consume the owner’s day, new sales alone may not create room to grow.

The question is which responsibility needs another owner. That might be prospect research, carrier coverage, onboarding, negotiation, or financial administration. Start by looking at the work rather than selecting the role that sounds most closely associated with growth.

sections.title: Understand the functions well enough to evaluate them.
paragraphs: The lesson describes Luis’s experience across accounting, dispatch, carrier negotiations, cold calls, claims, projects, and compliance. He uses that range to explain why an owner needs enough understanding to train and assess the work being delegated.

Understanding a function does not mean keeping it forever. The goal can be for the new person to become better at that work than the owner. What matters is being able to explain the task, recognize a complete result, and provide support when the ordinary process does not fit.

sections.title: Look for differences in strengths.
paragraphs: Luis’s example compares financial administration performed by his brother with the same work performed by him. Reviewing cash, balancing checks, and paying invoices took his brother much less time; compliance questions could produce the opposite pattern. The anecdote illustrates complementary strengths.

It is not a promise of a particular time saving from hiring. Use the principle to examine your own week. Which tasks repeatedly take you away from work you are better positioned to do? Which require a different kind of attention or skill? A clear pattern is more useful than the frustration of one difficult day.

sections.title: Describe the responsibility the person will own.
paragraphs: A request to help with operations is too broad to evaluate. Name the tasks and handoffs. For carrier coverage, what information arrives, which checks are required, who approves a booking, and how is the status recorded? For administration, what makes the shipment file complete?

The description helps both selection and training. It also reveals whether the work is actually ready to delegate. A new person should not have to infer instructions from fragments of the owner’s memory while being judged against expectations that were never stated.

sections.title: Build service capacity before expanding the team widely.
paragraphs: Luis cautions against recruiting many agents before learning how to support even one. House accounts and existing customers need dependable execution. The operating organization should demonstrate that it can support the commitments made by the sales side.

A first hire is an opportunity to test and improve the handoff. Learn where the instructions are unclear, where information is missing, and which decisions still come back to the owner. Those lessons can make later hiring more deliberate.

sections.title: Evaluate what changed after delegation.
paragraphs: The practical result should be more than an additional person in the business. Determine whether the assigned responsibility is being handled and whether the owner has gained capacity for the intended work. If every decision still returns to the same desk, the role or process may need adjustment.

Continue teaching and clarifying the handoff. The first hire does not have to solve every operating problem. It should solve a defined one well enough that the organization becomes more capable and the next growth decision is easier to assess.
